source.role: English objective and progression anchors only; Japanese scenes are original and Spanish currency, foods, and grammar are not copied

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Say breakfast words clearly and greet a server or barista politely in the morning.
lessons.title: Morning at the café
lessons.objective: Greet café staff politely, say your name, and recognize common breakfast words in hiragana and katakana.
lessons.focus: おはようございます is a polite morning greeting. は in わたしは is pronounced wa; です makes a polite statement. Long vowels matter in コーヒー. Katakana often marks loanwords such as コーヒー and メニュー.
lessons.scene: Sam enters a small café in the morning and asks about breakfast.

cards.note: Often written お茶; introduced in kana first.

cards.ja: ありがとうございます
よろしくおねがいします
cards.note: Contextual greeting, not a word-for-word equivalent.

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: おはようございます。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: おはようございます。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: わたしはサムです。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: サムさん、よろしくおねがいします。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: メニューはありますか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、こちらです。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: コーヒーとパンはありますか。
reader.en: Do you have coffee and bread?

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、あります。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: ありがとうございます。

speaking.opening: おはようございます。ご注文は何になさいますか。
speaking.goal: Greet the staff, say your name, and ask whether coffee and bread are available.
speaking.closure: Thank the staff politely; do not claim an order was placed unless it was confirmed.

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Use numbers, prices in pesos, clock times and café quantities to order and check a total.
lessons.title: Two coffees and the total
lessons.objective: Order two coffees and three pieces of bread using Japanese counters, then confirm a price in yen.
lessons.focus: Use コーヒーを二はい for two cups and パンを三つ for three general pieces. ですか asks for confirmation. 円 means yen; café prices vary, so the example total is fictional. The Spanish source's pesos are intentionally adapted to yen.
lessons.scene: Sam and a friend order at a café counter and check the stated total.

cards.ja: コーヒーを二はいください

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: おはようございます。ご注文は何になさいますか。
reader.en: Good morning. What would you like to order?

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: コーヒーを二はいください。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: パンを三つください。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: おいくらですか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: 千円です。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: 千円ですか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、そうです。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: ありがとうございます。

speaking.opening: おはようございます。ご注文は何になさいますか。
speaking.goal: Order two coffees and three pieces of bread; ask for and repeat the total in yen.
speaking.closure: Only confirm the price the partner actually states.

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Describe food, drinks and tables at a café with ser and estar.
lessons.title: A table and a hot coffee
lessons.objective: Ask whether a table is available and describe the temperature or taste of a drink or food without importing Spanish ser/estar grammar.
lessons.focus: Use この席は空いていますか to ask about seat availability. あつい describes a hot drink; つめたい describes a cold one. Japanese adjectives do not map onto the Spanish ser/estar distinction, so this lesson teaches predicate adjectives and current-state expressions instead.
lessons.scene: Sam asks for a table, then checks a coffee and a sweet pastry with the server.

cards.ja: この席は空いていますか
コーヒーはあついです

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: すみません。この席は空いていますか。
reader.en: Excuse me. Is this seat available?

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、空いています。どうぞ。
reader.en: Yes, it is available. Please go ahead.

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: ありがとうございます。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: コーヒーをどうぞ。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: このコーヒーはあついですね。
reader.en: This coffee is hot, isn't it?

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、あついです。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: このパンはあまいですか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、あまいです。

speaking.opening: いらっしゃいませ。お席をお探しですか。
speaking.goal: Ask whether a seat is free and describe whether your coffee is hot and bread is sweet.
speaking.closure: Thank the staff; avoid claiming any allergy accommodation.

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Say what you have, need and want at breakfast, and ask what the café has.
lessons.title: Ask what is available
lessons.objective: Say you are hungry, ask whether orange juice is available, and request a fork and napkin politely.
lessons.focus: ありますか asks whether an item is available. ほしいです expresses what you want; ～をください requests an item politely. Japanese does not copy Spanish tener/hay/querer conjugations. 「新鮮」 is not used to claim juice quality; ask whether it is freshly squeezed if that distinction matters.
lessons.scene: At the café counter, Sam asks about juice before requesting utensils.

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: すみません。おなかがすきました。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: ご注文は何になさいますか。
reader.en: What would you like to order?

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: オレンジジュースはありますか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、あります。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: しぼりたてですか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: いいえ、しぼりたてではありません。
reader.en: No, it is not freshly squeezed.

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: では、おちゃをください。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: フォークとナプキンもください。
reader.en: A fork and napkin too, please.

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、かしこまりました。

speaking.opening: おはようございます。ご注文は何になさいますか。
speaking.goal: Say you are hungry, ask whether orange juice is available, then request a fork and napkin. Confirm any quality claim before repeating it.
speaking.closure: Thank staff after the request is acknowledged.

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Say where you are going for breakfast, what you will order, and what you can do at a café.
lessons.title: Eat here or take away
lessons.objective: Say you plan to eat here and ask whether you may sit outside and pay by card.
lessons.focus: ここで食べます states where an action takes place. ～てもいいですか asks permission. カードで払えますか asks whether card payment is possible. A terrace or payment method is never assumed available.
lessons.scene: Sam arrives at a café with outside seating and checks the choices before ordering.

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: 店内でお召し上がりですか。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: はい、ここで食べます。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: 外の席に座ってもいいですか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、今は空いています。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: コーヒーを注文します。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: かしこまりました。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: カードで払えますか。

reader.speaker: Staff
reader.ja: はい、レジで払えます。
reader.en: Yes, you can pay at the register.

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: ありがとうございます。

speaking.opening: いらっしゃいませ。店内でお召し上がりですか。
speaking.goal: Say you will eat here, ask permission to sit outside, and check whether card payment is available.
speaking.closure: Confirm the staff response before moving outside or paying.

lessons.sourceEnglishObjective: Talk about what you eat and drink for breakfast using present-tense verbs.
lessons.title: What do you have for breakfast?
lessons.objective: Tell another guest what you usually eat and drink, and ask about their breakfast.
lessons.focus: Japanese polite nonpast ～ます covers habits and future context; it does not inflect by person like Spanish present-tense verbs. いつも means usually; 毎朝 means every morning. を marks what is eaten or drunk. Avoid assuming another guest lives locally.
lessons.scene: Two guests talk over breakfast in a hotel dining room.

reader.speaker: Guest
reader.ja: おはようございます。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: おはようございます。

reader.speaker: Guest
reader.ja: 朝ごはんは何を食べますか。
reader.en: What do you eat for breakfast?

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: いつもパンとたまごを食べます。
reader.en: I usually eat bread and eggs.

reader.speaker: Guest
reader.ja: コーヒーとおちゃ、どちらを飲みますか。
reader.en: Which do you drink, coffee or tea?

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: 朝ごはんは何を食べますか。

reader.speaker: Guest
reader.ja: ごはんとたまごを食べます。

reader.speaker: Sam
reader.ja: ありがとうございます。

speaking.opening: おはようございます。朝ごはんは何を食べますか。
speaking.goal: Describe your usual breakfast and ask whether the other guest drinks coffee or tea.
speaking.closure: End the conversation politely without asking where the guest lives.
